primary_topics: Chapter 16 of 'Love God, Serve Man' -- CJP's reaction paper of March 15, 1994 at the UP Law Center, delivered at the Phi Kappa Phi (UP Chapter) 60th anniversary roundtable on Dr. F. Landa Jocano's thesis that traditional values have positive roles in stimulating industrialization and that the lack of appreciation of those roles is what impedes rapid economic growth.

His central qualification: he can accept the first half of Jocano's thesis but not 'the rather absolutist and exclusivistic implication of the second part' -- the lack of appreciation of traditional values is one factor impeding growth, but neither the only nor the most critical one.

The Catholic perspective: PCP II's teaching that it is not Filipino values themselves but 'the exaggeration and the wrong uses we have put them to' that breed inequality, its demand for an inculturated faith, its verdict that 'our society remains a sick society,' and its calls for re-evangelization and total integral development.

The businessman's and lawyer's perspectives: that the diagnosis should focus on the last 25-30 years rather than the last century, that the Filipino is productive and law-abiding abroad because rewards differ there rather than because of native values, that the three L's of LUSOT, LAKAS and LAGAY have replaced hard work and discipline, and that the Constitution, statutes and Supreme Court have in fact absorbed indigenous values into the legal system.
sub_topics: He states Jocano's thesis and his own line of attack -- agreeing that traditional values have positive roles, but contesting the implication that their unappreciated state is 'the single force or matter' inhibiting development -- then announces his three perspectives: Catholic layman, part-time businessman, full-time practising lawyer.

As a Catholic, he notes the Church asks the same question Jocano does: why a country 'so rich in potential, is so poor in reality,' and why a Christian people is 'so afflicted with violence, poverty and injustice.'

He describes PCP II (January 20 to February 17, 1991) as the Church's equivalent of a constitutional convention, the first time in 2,000 years that laymen, laywomen and ordinary priests took part in the Church's lawmaking, and counts himself fortunate to have been a lay delegate.

He quotes PCP II's own position on values: after EDSA the realization grew that 'change in social structures is not enough without change too in cultural values,' but 'it is not our values so much that are at fault as the exaggeration and the wrong uses we have put them to,' whose excess produces gross economic and political inequalities and political dynasties.
He cites PCP II on inculturation: faith 'must take root in the matrix of our Filipino being,' presented 'with tools, methods and expressions coming from the culture itself.'

He confronts the paradox that over 90 percent of Filipinos profess Christ -- the God who preached sharing and condemned violence and corruption -- yet the only Christian nation in Asia is also 'the poorest, most violent, most graft-ridden,' quoting PCP II that despite full churches 'our society remains a sick society.'

He gives the Church's explanation -- Christians who lead 'dichotomized lives,' Christian in faith but not in deeds, in church but not in their offices and government jobs -- and PCP II's remedy of massive re-evangelization.

He sets out PCP II's decree of total integral development: a Christian must act out his faith in every sphere, the Church must be wherever there is sinfulness and injustice, and the reforms were to be in place ten years from 1991.

Turning to business, he challenges Jocano's 100-year frame: up to the late '60s the Philippines was 'the show window of democracy in Asia,' with the peso under four to the dollar, single-digit inflation, interest rates below 10 percent, public high schools matching the best universities and minimal corruption -- so 'We must have been doing right then what we are doing wrong now,' and the values study should cover only the last 25-30 years.

He argues the Filipino remains 'teachable, productive, diligent, self-reliant and law-abiding' -- outearning white-skinned counterparts in the US, outproducing others in the Middle East, trusted with children in Hong Kong -- yet performs worse at home, and asks whether the real cause is that productivity and good citizenship bring no prosperity in his own country.

He illustrates the malaise with Kardo, his favorite taxi driver, who in 20 years of weaving through traffic and running red lights has never been issued a traffic violation receipt, and who explains his method in three stages: LUSOT (talking his way out), LAKAS (name-dropping Major Cruz, the traffic chief, with photo and calling card) and LAGAY (the 'lawyers' Quezon, Osmena, Roxas and Ninoy Aquino, alive in one's wallet).

He draws the conclusion that the three L's 'have taken the place of hard work, discipline and obedience to law,' making virtue and talent less useful than talk, influence and bribery for securing jobs, profits and approvals.

He questions whether Jocano's cultural ideals and core values -- galang, pagbabahala, pananagutan, balikatan, bayanihan, malasakit, asal, halaga, diwa, hiya, delikadesa, utang na loob and the rest -- are not 'basically Tagalog' and preponderant only in Tagalog-speaking regions, then declines to enter the debate on the national language and soul.

As a lawyer of 33 years he answers Jocano's claim of an exogenous, adversarial legal model at odds with an indigenous, consensual community: borrowing from colonizers' legal systems is common, and Philippine law has been calibrated to local custom -- no absolute divorce, mutual support between spouses and between parents and children, Muslim Shari'a Courts, autonomous governments in the Cordilleras and Mindanao, and the Local Government Code -- to the point that he wonders whether such localization now impedes globalization.

He shows the 1987 Constitution embedding cultural values: the sanctity of family life and total human liberation in Art. II; 'pananagutan' as accountability and 'public office is a public trust' in Art. XI; 'pagbabahala' and 'malasakit' in Art. XII's equitable distribution of opportunities, income and wealth; and 'balikatan' and 'bayanihan' in the cutting down of presidential power, the consensual legislature, judicial review of grave abuse, and the independence of the COA, Civil Service and Comelec.

He shows the Supreme Court's sensitivity to the social environment through three cases -- Rubi vs. Provincial Board of Mindoro (1919), upholding a reservation law that would shock civil libertarians today, as retired Justice Jose C. Campos Jr. observed; Villavicencio vs. Lukban, decided weeks later, striking down the deportation of women of ill repute from Manila on liberty-of-abode grounds; and Central Mindanao University vs. DARAB (October 22, 1992), voiding the distribution of a state university's land reservation -- concluding that the Court decides 'not in isolation but in magisterial consideration of contemporaneous situations.'

In summary he concedes that lack of appreciation of traditional values is 'one factor' but 'not the most critical one'; reports the Church's call for inculturated re-evangelization, quoting Archbishop Leonardo Legaspi that through gospel values 'the structures of injustice and corruption in our midst can be firmly dismantled'; observes empirically that the Filipino's prosperity abroad cannot be credited to Tagalog, Cebuano or Maranaw values but to 'the more Western reward system for work well done'; and closes as a lawyer with Dean Roscoe Pound's advice that 'Law must be stable, but it cannot stand still.'

stances.claim: Lack of appreciation of traditional values is one factor impeding rapid economic growth but not the only nor the most critical one, so Jocano's thesis is too absolutist in its second half.
stances.rhetorical_move: concede-then-qualify: accepting the first clause of the thesis in order to attack the exclusivity of the second

stances.claim: It is not Filipino values that are at fault but their exaggeration and abuse, and the Church's answer is a massive re-evangelization in inculturated form, since Filipinos lead dichotomized lives -- Christian in faith but not in deeds.
stances.rhetorical_move: conciliar-citation: letting PCP II's own text carry the diagnosis and remedy

stances.claim: The values inquiry should cover the last 25-30 years, not the last 100, because until the late '60s the Philippines led the region -- 'We must have been doing right then what we are doing wrong now.'
stances.rhetorical_move: periodization challenge backed by remembered indicators (exchange rate, inflation, interest, schooling)

stances.claim: The Filipino's productivity abroad cannot be credited to his traditional values, which are not observed in his foreign workplace, but to a Western reward system for work well done.
stances.rhetorical_move: empirical-inversion: using the overseas worker as a natural experiment against the values hypothesis

stances.claim: LUSOT, LAKAS and LAGAY have displaced hard work, discipline and obedience to law as the means of getting ahead in the Philippines.
stances.rhetorical_move: anecdote-to-diagnosis: Kardo the taxi driver's three-stage escape generalized into a national malaise

stances.claim: Where values are critical to national welfare, the framers, the lawmakers and the Supreme Court have already written them into the legal system, breaking the supposed barrier between the exogenous and indigenous models.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional-and-case inventory: matching each Filipino value to a specific provision or decision

notable_anecdotes: Kardo's three L's: his favorite taxi driver explains, in Tagalog, how twenty years of red lights and counterflow have never earned him a ticket -- first LUSOT by pleading and arguing, then LAKAS with a photo and calling card from Major Cruz the traffic chief, and finally LAGAY.
The lawyers in the wallet: asked how dead presidents can still serve as his lawyers, Kardo answers 'Aba, buhay ho sila. Buksan ninyo ang wallet ninyo at makikita ninyo sila doon!'
The rollback adjustment: Kardo notes that recently, before the rollback, he had been forced to promote Ninoy Aquino to the role of lawyer.
Sitting as a lay delegate: CJP recalls being one of the laymen admitted for the first time in 2,000 years to the Church's lawmaking at PCP II.

The show window remembered: he recounts the Philippines of the late '60s -- under four pesos to the dollar, single-digit inflation, public high schools as good as Jesuit or Dominican universities -- when Asian neighbors sent students here to copy Filipino institutions.

Two decisions a month apart: he contrasts Rubi (1919), upholding confinement of a non-Christian tribe to a reservation, with Villavicencio vs. Lukban weeks later, striking down the Manila mayor's deportation of women to Davao.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 16 of 'Love God, Serve Man' is the reaction paper CJP delivered on March 15, 1994 at the UP Law Center, at the Phi Kappa Phi 60th anniversary roundtable on Dr. F. Landa Jocano's thesis that traditional values have positive roles in stimulating industrialization and that the lack of appreciation of those roles impedes rapid growth. He accepted the first half but attacked 'the rather absolutist and exclusivistic implication of the second,' and answered from three perspectives. As a Catholic layman he reported PCP II's inquiry into why a country so rich in potential is so poor in reality, quoting its finding that 'it is not our values so much that are at fault as the exaggeration and the wrong uses we have put them to,' its insistence on an inculturated faith, its verdict that 'our society remains a sick society' despite full churches, its diagnosis of dichotomized Christians, and its prescriptions of re-evangelization and total integral development. As a businessman he challenged Jocano's century-long frame, recalling that until the late '60s the Philippines was the show window of democracy in Asia -- under four pesos to the dollar, single-digit inflation, public schools as good as the best universities -- so that the study should cover only the last 25-30 years; and he argued that the Filipino is productive, diligent and law-abiding abroad yet not at home, which points to reward systems rather than native values. He illustrated the malaise with Kardo, the taxi driver who escapes every ticket by LUSOT, LAKAS and finally LAGAY, the dead presidents in his wallet serving as his lawyers, and asked whether Jocano's core values were not basically Tagalog. As a lawyer of 33 years he showed that Philippine law has been calibrated to local custom, that the 1987 Constitution encodes pananagutan, malasakit, balikatan and bayanihan, and that the Supreme Court decides with an eye to contemporaneous conditions, closing with Roscoe Pound's 'Law must be stable, but it cannot stand still.'
